cards.explanation: The answer is more than all their fathers. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, is king in Judah, and the text says their sins “…provoked Him to jealous anger more than all their fathers had done.” That's a heavy line, friends, and I think it's meant to be.

The answer is False. Judah's worship under King Rehoboam looks a lot like those nations. The text says Judah “…imitated all the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.” Judah copied what those nations had done. It's a sobering verse, friends, and the text doesn't soften it.

The answer is the treasures of the temple and the palace. Shishak, Egypt's king, grabbed the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the royal palace. The text says he “took everything.” I think the king of Egypt came to Jerusalem with a very big bag.
The answer is bronze. Shishak, Egypt's king, had taken the gold shields Solomon had made, so Rehoboam made bronze ones in their place. Same job, less shine. Gold to bronze is a rough trade, friends.

The answer is back to the guardroom. The guards bore the shields whenever the king entered the house of the LORD, and later they returned them to the guardroom. So the shields were brought out for the king's visits and then put away. I think that's a lot of walking for a shield that isn't gold.

The answer is True. The text says, “There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.” Jeroboam was the king of Israel, the northern kingdom. Two kings, friends, and war between them throughout their days.

The answer is the City of David. The text says Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David. Rehoboam is Solomon's son, as the text says when it introduces him. The City of David is the place the text names.

The answer is in all the sins of his father. The text says Abijam, Rehoboam's son, “…walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed…” He didn't pick up one or two of his father's sins, friends. He took the whole set.

The answer is David. The text says Abijam's heart “…was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God as the heart of David his forefather had been.” David was the standard the writer measures him against. Abijam came up short.

The answer is a son to succeed him and make Jerusalem strong. The text says the LORD gave Abijam a lamp in Jerusalem “…by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong.” The lamp is a son, and Asa is that son. The text says the LORD did it for the sake of David.

The answer is Uriah. The text says David “…had not turned aside from anything the LORD commanded all the days of his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.” The writer doesn't hide it, and he doesn't make a big speech about it either. The one exception is named plainly.

The answer is False. The war does not end. The text says, “…there was war between the houses of Rehoboam and Jeroboam all the days of Abijam’s life.” Abijam, Rehoboam's son, took the throne, but the fighting didn't change hands with it. It carried right on.

The answer is Maacah daughter of Abishalom. The text says Asa's grandmother's name was Maacah daughter of Abishalom. Remember that name, friends, because she comes up again in this passage. Things get personal for Asa.

The answer is True. The text says, “And Asa did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as his father David had done.” Asa was king of Judah, and after two kings who walked in sin, this is a change. I'd call it a nice change.

The answer is False. Asa doesn't leave them standing. The text says Asa “…removed all the idols that his fathers had made.” That's every one of them. Asa also banished the male shrine prostitutes from the land.

The answer is that he removes her as queen mother. Asa removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. I think that cost him something, friends. It's not easy when the problem has your own family name on it.
The answer is False. The text says, “The high places were not removed…” Asa did a lot of clean-up, but this was left standing. Even good kings in the text don't finish everything.

The answer is fully devoted to the LORD all his days. The text says that although the high places were not removed, “…Asa’s heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his days.” The writer says it plainly and doesn't hedge. Abijam's heart, by contrast, was not as fully devoted as the heart of David.

The answer is entering. Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah “…to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah.” The text pairs leaving with entering, friends. Entering is the word.

The answer is Ben-hadad king of Aram. Asa sent his servants with the silver and gold to Ben-hadad, who was ruling in Damascus. Asa was asking a foreign king for help. The silver and gold went along with a message.

The answer is to break his treaty with Baasha king of Israel. Asa's message says, “Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me.” The silver and gold were a gift sent along with that request. The whole ask is in that one line.

The answer is False. Ben-hadad doesn't turn Asa down. The text says Ben-hadad “…listened to King Asa…” and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel. That's the opposite of staying loyal to Baasha. He conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and the whole land of Naphtali.

The answer is True. The text says, “When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah.” He stopped as soon as he learned of it, friends. By then, Ben-hadad's commanders were conquering cities of Israel.

The answer is that they carry off its stones and timbers. King Asa summoned all the men of Judah, with no exceptions, and they “…carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building.” Stones and timbers, all hauled off. With no exceptions is how the text puts it.

The answer is that he builds up Geba and Mizpah. With the materials Baasha had used for building, King Asa built up Geba of Benjamin, as well as Mizpah. Those same stones and timbers went to work on Geba and Mizpah, friends.
The answer is False. The text says, “In his old age, however, he became diseased in his feet.” I think that's a hard note to end on, friends, and the text just states it.
The answer is Jehoshaphat. After Asa rested with his fathers, his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place. Asa's long reign ended and the throne passed down once more. The line of David kept going.
